▸Overview & logins

What this is: a real, running AAP environment built for two example tenants, tenant-a and tenant-b. You will log in as different people and watch what changes. Every screenshot below is from this live system.
Logins you will use (password for all: password):
UserWho they areWhat to expect
adminPlatform administratorSees and manages everything
tenant-a-adminTenant A's adminFull control — but only inside tenant-a
tenant-a-user1Tenant A's operatorCan run tenant-a automation, cannot change it
tenant-b-adminTenant B's adminA mirror world — only tenant-b

★The big idea — 4 building blocks

BlockPlain meaningIn this pilot
OrganizationThe tenant's walled garden — nothing inside is visible outsidetenant-a, tenant-b
Team & UserThe people in the gardentenant-a-team: admin + user1
RoleWhat each person may do: view / run / changeOrg Admin vs Org Member
Instance GroupWhich machine the tenant's jobs run onig-tenant-a → exec-a only

Organization — the SEE boundary. Think of an organization as a walled garden. Every automation object (project, inventory, credential, job template) is planted inside exactly one garden, and the platform only ever shows you the gardens you belong to. This is why a tenant-a user doesn't just get “access denied” on tenant-b's automation — they don't even know it exists: lists come back filtered, and a direct request by ID is answered with 403.

Role — the DO permission. Being inside the garden tells you nothing about what you may touch. That's the role's job. An Organization Admin owns the garden: create, edit, delete, manage members. An Organization Member may only look — and then specific team grants add narrowly-scoped abilities on individual objects, such as “execute this job template” or “use this credential”. That combination is what produces a safe operator: someone who can run approved automation all day without being able to break it.

Instance Group — the WHERE guarantee. Visibility and permissions control people; the instance group controls machines. Each tenant org is bound to its own instance group containing only that tenant's execution node, and the job templates are pinned to it. So even when both tenants run jobs at the same moment, the workloads execute on physically different servers — no shared CPU, memory, or job queue between tenants.

💡 RBAC concept Memorize one line: Organization decides what you can SEE, Role decides what you can DO, Instance Group decides WHERE your jobs run. The 10 steps below prove each part.

1Log in — one front door for everyone

Do this: Open https://aap.redhat.local. Log in as admin / password.

💡 RBAC concept The Platform Gateway is the single entry point and the authority that enforces RBAC on every page and API call.

2See the tenants — Organizations

Do this: As admin, go to Access Management → Organizations.

💡 RBAC concept An Organization is the tenant boundary. Everything a tenant owns (projects, credentials, templates) lives inside its org — and is invisible to other orgs.

3See the people — Users

Do this: Still as admin, go to Access Management → Users.

💡 RBAC concept A User gets nothing by default. Power comes from the Role they hold in an organization: Organization Admin = manage everything in the org; Organization Member = view + the team's run permissions.

4See the dedicated machines — Instance Groups

Do this: Go to Automation Execution → Infrastructure → Instance Groups.

💡 RBAC concept An Instance Group pins a tenant's jobs to specific machines. tenant-a's templates may only run on exec-a; tenant-b's only on exec-b. That is the “dedicated resources” guarantee.

5Log in as the tenant admin

Do this: Log out, log back in as tenant-a-admin. Open Automation Execution → Templates.

💡 RBAC concept This is visibility scoping: the platform only lists resources from organizations you belong to. tenant-b's automation simply does not exist for this user.

6Now the same page as the operator

Do this: Log out, log in as tenant-a-user1. Open the same Templates page.

Compare steps 5 and 6 — this picture summarizes the difference. Both users stand in the same garden (org tenant-a), so both see the same resources. What separates them is the verbs: the admin's role adds edit / create / manage on top of view + run, while the operator gets view + run and nothing more. And for both of them, tenant-b's garden is not just locked — it's invisible:

💡 RBAC concept Same organization, different Role. The operator holds Organization Member plus a team grant to execute this template and use this credential — so they can run automation but never modify it. Notice this is least privilege done with built-in roles only: no custom role engineering was needed to get a safe operator profile.

7Prove it — try to create a Project as each user

Do this: As each user, go to Automation Execution → Projects and look for the Create button.

What just happened behind the scenes? Every request — from the UI or the raw API — goes through the same decision. The gateway first establishes who you are (one login for the whole platform), then checks which role you hold in the organization that owns the object, and only then lets the action through:

💡 RBAC concept Authorization is enforced on the action, not just hidden in the UI. Greyed-out buttons are a courtesy; the real gate is the API answering 201 Created for the admin and 403 Forbidden for the operator. That matters for security reviews: you cannot bypass RBAC by calling the API directly, scripting, or using the CLI — it is the same check everywhere.

8Run automation the self-service way

Do this: As tenant-a-user1, click the launch (rocket) button on tenant-a-hello.

💡 RBAC concept Self-service: the admin pre-approves the automation and decides which inputs to expose; the operator just fills a simple form. No Ansible knowledge needed — and they still cannot touch the code behind it.

9Check the job — it ran on tenant-a's OWN server

Do this: Open the finished job and look at the Details and Output tabs.

This is the “dedicated resources” half of the story. RBAC keeps people apart; the instance group keeps workloads apart. When the template launches, the controller looks at which instance group it is pinned to and schedules the job only on machines in that group — and tenant-a's group contains exactly one machine: its own execution node:

💡 RBAC concept Dedicated execution: the org's Instance Group decides WHERE jobs run. Verified live: tenant-a's job ran on exec-a (172.16.28.31), tenant-b's on exec-b (172.16.28.32). Even under load, one tenant can never consume the other's execution capacity — there is no shared job queue between them.

10Switch tenants — a mirror world

Do this: Log in as tenant-b-admin and open Templates.

💡 RBAC concept Complete two-way isolation. Even both tenants' git repositories are separate: each project pulls from its own private repo with its own credential — tenant-a's git token gets 404 on tenant-b's repo.

All of the above was verified live by an automated test (playbooks/validate.yml) that logs in as each user via the API: isolation PASS · dedicated-execution PASS. The whole setup — organizations, teams, users, roles, instance groups, projects, surveys — is defined as code and can be re-applied or rebuilt at any time.

AAP 2.7 (containerized) on RHEL 9.7, VMware vSphere · one all-in-one node + one dedicated execution node per tenant · RBAC defined as code with ansible.platform / ansible.controller.
